dossier.public_summary: The dip is on the star and is flat and planet-sized, but its depth changes dramatically between TESS sectors, it shows a huge brightness swing outside the dips, and the star itself is a high-noise astrometric binary with an unusually long duration. Together this is best explained as ellipsoidal or spot-linked variability from a close binary, not a 13-hour planet.

reasons.why: Depth changes strongly between sectors (47.29 chi2, dof 3, depth_change_pct 75.82). Tool sector_depths_by_source gives changes_within_a_source with p_constant_all 2.7546523066732613e-10 and TESS-SPOC p_constant 1.6871457194230568e-06, ruling out calibration difference and directly favouring a non-planet that looks different when the aperture/context changes.
Huge out-of-dip swing at this period, almost as big as the dip itself, is typical of ellipsoidal/reflection or spot modulation from a close binary/variability, not a planet transit.

Duration much longer than central for a 0.7524 Rsun star, mirrored by Gaia excess_noise_sig 935, ruwe 7.368 and star_density_penalty 705.2, pointing to the stellar density being misinterpreted – best explained by spurious or out-of-aperture dips.

Very high RUWE plus huge Gaia excess noise positively indicates the target is an astrometric binary/variable, consistent with the phase-curve and sector-depth variability rather than a quiet planet host.
Individual transits are inconsistent (outliers at 3140 ppm and 3226 ppm sigma 4.3), supporting depth scatter as astrophysical/systematic, not Poisson noise around a stable planet.
